title: Reflections on Our Practice
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of the Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of embracing an active and embodied approach to meditation (zazen), rather than trying to achieve a specific state or understanding through intellectual means. Dogen's teachings encourage us to let go of conceptual frameworks and expectations, instead cultivating a "no-thinking" approach that allows us to tap into our true nature and engage with the world in a way that sees everything as inherently complete and Buddha-like. By embracing this approach, we can make space for our true nature to express itself freely, without attachment or expectation.

sentences.text: Well, I thought we might reflect a little today on our wonderful and not understandable practice.
All we have are words and concepts, but they can support us and connect us and inspire us even if they're limited and never quite exactly clear or right.
Raizelah and I went down to California a couple weeks ago for the Every Day Zen annual five-day sesshin.
They do it at a Catholic retreat center called Santa Sabina.
Nice place.
In his talks, Norman spoke about Dogen's fascicle Zazen-shin in Bendoah, which means something like the point of zazen.
So I was thinking about what Norman shared with us and the experience of hearing it.
Then I picked up Suzuki Roshi's Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind to think about whether I want to continue wending our way through that.
I had started going through it very carefully and slowly in lots of talks last year.
Then practice period happened and other things wanted to be said.
I still had open on my computer [unclear: "Dogen Leighton's"] essay called Zazen as Enactment Ritual.
All these things seem to be pointing in the same direction, and all of them are hard to pin down or make sense of or understand in that usual way that we try to understand things.
All these teachings just don't lend themselves to any kind of simple explanation of what this is and why we're doing it.
And yet we all have our reasons, and each of us could easily come up with some simple things to say.
Maybe you feel it calms you down to sit in silence: what a relief from the busy ways that we are and experience most of the time.
Maybe you appreciate the community of people who share an interest in this.
Maybe you appreciate the teachings of Buddhism, and being involved in a Buddhist group seems like a good way to access that.
But the truth seems to be that our practice can't really be held or contained or understood through a simple idea, or through any ideas.
There's a touching into something that we feel deeply and can't quite explain.
Language and concepts, which are all we have, by their nature divide things and describe things and separate things, and that just doesn't seem to quite do it.
So in Dogen's Zazen-shin, he opens this chapter on the point of Zazen with the same koan that he references in Fukan Zazengi that we chant, which is this.
Yaoshan, great master Hongdo, was sitting.
The teacher was sitting.
*A monk asked him, in steadfast sitting, what do you think?
Yaoshan said, think not thinking.
The monk asked, how do you think not thinking?
Yaoshan replied, non thinking.*
How do you use your mind in Zazen?
Teacher says, think not thinking.
Monk asks, how do you think not thinking?
Teacher replies, non thinking.
I've seen various attempts to translate this.
But from my little research, this pairing of non thinking and not thinking is actually quite accurate to the Japanese and the underlying Chinese.
There's a particle at the beginning, before thinking, that means negation, and there's a couple of different ones, like not and non.
Not, non, no, un, we have a lot of them.
So it's two of those.
Different, but the same, right?
Both negation, but different.
And hearing this again as Norman read it, I realized that there's an important point here, before we get lost in what the heck, not thinking, non thinking, no, da, da, da, da, da.
Before all that, Yaoshan in his first instruction has an active verb, which is think.
That doesn't match the sort of popular imagination about meditation, right?
It's not about thinking.
It's about stopping the thinking, or ignoring the thinking, or letting the thinking flow.
This teacher actually said you should think.
So there's an activeness, an engagement, an entering, a bringing of energy.
Maybe not quite doing something, because we're not really doing, but we're thinking something called not thinking, which is like not-dash-thinking.
A certain kind of thinking, which is not thinking.
And so the monk asked on our behalf how on earth do you do that, how do you think not thinking, non thinking.
So I was thinking about this, and it was something that was kind of interesting to me anyway: the other option is think thinking, right?
Which is what we usually would do.
We usually think thinking, or the thinking thinks us.
That's an important and useful tool, essential to our living in this world.
But it's also very sticky and confusing, and we glom onto thoughts, we identify with thoughts, we believe in thoughts.
We get tumbled around by our thoughts.
Thoughts come unbidden and trigger suffering in us.
Someone was just talking to me about a situation where there's no clear path to do anything, but the mind just keeps trying to think about it, think about it.
There's got to be a way to do this right or solve this, but it doesn't appear to be, and the thinking just keeps thinking.
So that's thinking thinking, right?
So not thinking must be engaging with the thoughts the other way around, turning those thoughts in some way.
The opposite of all that.
So thinking thoughts, not stuck on thoughts.
Thinking thoughts, not identified with thoughts.
Thinking thoughts, not believing in thoughts.
Thinking thoughts, not being tumbled around by thoughts.
But there's thinking.
And doing this practice, says Dogen, after he quotes this koan, he says this:
*Realizing these words of Yaoshan, you should investigate and receive the authentic transmission of steadfast sitting.
This is the thorough study of steadfast sitting transmitted in the Buddha way.
Yaoshan is not the only one who spoke of thinking in steadfast sitting, but his words were extraordinary.
Think not thinking is the flesh, skin, flesh, bones and marrow of thinking and the skin, flesh, bones and marrow of not thinking.*
So Dogen often gets enthusiastic about things, but this is very enthusiastic.
This is really saying this is very important: think not thinking.

The other thing that's interesting about Zazen-shin is that he has two, maybe more, it's sometimes hard to figure out everything that's being said, but there are two clear places where he brings up what Zazen isn't.
That's a similar kind of move: you can't exactly say what not thinking is, but we can say what thinking is.
So it seems important that in this essay, a pretty important essay about Zazen, he chooses two things to warn us about specifically.
The first is:
*However careless students in recent times say, the endeavor of Zazen is completed when your heart is quiescent as Zazen is a place of calmness.*
So he's saying that's wrong.
It's not right to think or say that the endeavor of Zazen is completed when your heart is quiet, quiescent, and that Zazen is a place of calmness.
Zazen is not just resting in peacefulness, because that's not engaged.
That lacks that active verb.
Zazen is in fact radically engaged with experience, with aliveness, with being, with Buddha.
And then he goes on, I won't read this part, but he goes on about the bald-headed rascals again in China that think that way.
I wonder if the whole time in China he was just kind of looking around, grouching to himself,
until he met his teacher and then he felt good, who knows.
And here's his second example.
That was his first example of foolish views, that Zazen is just about calmness and peace.
The second example is:
*There are also people who say, practicing Zazen is essential for those who are beginners or those who have started studying recently, but is not necessarily the activity of Buddha ancestors.
Activity in daily life is Zen, and sitting is Zen.
In speaking and in silence, in motion and stillness, your body should be tranquil.
Do not be concerned only with the practice of Zazen.*
So the foolish view, number two, is that practicing Zazen is essential for beginners, those who have just started, but not necessarily the activity of Buddha ancestors, meaning mature teachers.
You don't have to worry about it too much, because activity in daily life is Zen.
Speaking, silence, motion, stillness, body, tranquil, all of it is Zen.
Don't be concerned only with the practice of Zazen.
So we know this view, the idea that everything is practice.
And if we don't really get around that often to formal sitting and structured practice at the Zendo, that's okay, because everything is practice, everything is Zen, and I'm always practicing.
And maybe a worse idea in there is that I'm now a mature student and I don't need to do this anymore, which is kind of arrogant.
So in this case, Dogen actually doesn't just throw all of China under the bus.
He throws Rinzai Zen under the bus for that one.
I don't know why exactly Rinzai Zen.
Rinzai people, I know [unclear: "Sid Zazen"] plenty, but he does.
And then, really interestingly, he pulls apart this idea of beginners.
So perhaps this inspired Suzuki Roshi much later.
He says, well, this idea that Zazen is for beginners, who are beginners?
Are there any who are not beginners?
When do you leave the beginner's mind?
*Know that in the definitive study of the Buddha Dharma, you engage in Zazen and endeavor in the way.
At the heart of the teaching is a practicing Buddha who does not seek to become a Buddha.*
So a Buddha that is always a beginner, in other words.
We're all beginners here.
That's for sure.
Don't you feel that?
I feel that.
We're totally beginners, if that.
I was kind of surprised by a nice compliment I got about this recently, because I don't know that I always feel like I hold this beginner's mind that well.
I've been slowly working with a teacher who is in the Rinzai koan introspection system, the Korean branch of it, but the Rinzai linji lineage.
And she gave me a nice compliment.

She said that although she sees me as a seasoned teacher, she experiences me as open-minded, curious, ready to learn more about Zen, learning about these koans and practicing with them, and humble as a beginner.
That was nice, because I mostly feel clueless when I'm working with her on koans.
And I noticed that before I meet with her, I always feel a little bit of dread.
Like, oh no, this is going to be frustrating, and I'll feel ignorant.
But I've also noticed that that dread vanishes as soon as we start exploring together.
We meet for like half an hour every couple of weeks on Zoom, and at the end of the exploration, I always feel really good.
So it's interesting, the suffering of anticipation, but that's maybe a little sidebar.
So maybe we're doing okay on this point, staying beginners.
So probably the first point is our point to work on.
Zazen is active engagement, but active engagement without expectation.
Without expectation.
To get at that idea, Dogen quotes a second koan in this essay.
You probably remember this story, too.
It's a story of when Master Matsu was a student studying with his teacher, Nanyue.
*After intimately receiving Nanyue's mind seal, Matsu was continuously engaged in Zazen.
One day Nanyue went up to him and said,*
*Virtuous one, what is your intention in doing Zazen?
Matsu said, my intention is to become a Buddha.
So Nanyue picked up a rock, picked up a tile, and started to polish it with a rock.
Matsu said, what are you doing?
Nanyue said, I'm polishing this tile to make a mirror.
Matsu said, how can you make a mirror by polishing a tile?
To which Nanyue said, how can you become a Buddha by teaching, by doing Zazen?*
Wonderful story.
What I didn't know, because I think it's maybe in the Blue Cliff record version, maybe, but whoever Dogen was sourcing this from, he has more.
So here's the next part.
Matsu says, then how so?
How do you become a Buddha or make a mirror?
So Nanyue asked a question:
*When driving a cart, if it stops moving, do you whip the cart or the ox?
When driving a cart, if it stops moving, do you whip the cart or whip the ox?*
So of course, like you, Matsu can see the obvious answer and realizes there's something else going on here.
Since he had already learned some things that confused him, he was silent, didn't answer.
And Nanyue instructed: *if you practice sitting Zen, you practice sitting Buddha.* Sitting Zen, sitting Buddha.
So practice, engaged; sitting, engaged.
And then it doesn't really matter if it's Zen or Buddha, mirror or tile.
Fully engaged, but not thinking the engagement makes something happen.
And of course, in the conventional world, we all know full well
you can't make a mirror by polishing a tile.
So therefore, you can't make a Buddha by sitting in Zazen.
But Dogen, as he likes to, doesn't let us stand pat in that simple position either, because there's still a separation there in saying, oh, I'll just sit.
He says, well no, actually that's exactly how mirrors are created.
Here's what he wrote:
*Polishing a tile to make a mirror has a deep meaning.
It is not a false statement, but actualizes the fundamental point.
Although a tile is a tile and a mirror is a mirror, there are many ways to investigate the meaning of polishing.
An ancient bright mirror comes from polishing a tile.*
That's where the ancient bright mirror comes from, polishing a tile.
*Without knowing that all mirrors come from polishing tiles, you will not see the words, mouth, or breath of Buddha ancestors.* So it's not just that way either.
Suzuki Roshi talks about what we get from all this in this way.
In Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, the next part, which is called Nothing Special, he said:
*If you continue this simple practice every day, you will attain a wonderful power.
Before you attain it, you think it's something wonderful anyway.
But after you attain it, it is nothing special, nothing special at all.*
You're like, wait a minute, what?
So wonderful and nothing special.

Paralleling all this in Fukan Zazengi, the other great essay on Zazen from Dogen, *Now that you've taken all this in, therefore, you should therefore cease from practice based on intellectual understanding, pursuing words and following after speech, and learn the backward step that turns your light inwardly to illuminate yourself.
Body and mind of themselves will drop away and your original face will be manifest.
If you want to attain suchness, you should practice suchness without delay.*
What I noticed is that for those of us who chanted this one, we've chanted this over and over, some of us.
It starts to sound like music, which it is.
It's beautiful music.
But can we really take in the meaning?
Our habit of think-thinking is so powerful, and of course we apply it to practice and life and all of our problems and our suffering.
But can we cease from that?
Can we think not thinking instead?
Cease from practice based on intellect, words, speech?
And take a backward step.
Turns the light inwardly, so like turning the thoughts around.
Think not thinking, instead of think thinking.
And maybe when Dogen turns the koan around, and that's what he usually does, he lets us hang out in the usual understanding and then tells us the other way around.
Maybe what he's trying to whisper to us through the ages is, "Don't be so sure."
Maybe that's what Dogen's trying to say.
Don't be so sure.
Concepts, assumptions, perceptions, ideas, self.
The usual reading of a koan, that you can't make a mirror out of a tile, can't make a Buddha from zazen, is fine, but the opposite is also important, also true.
Buddhas come from practice, ancient bright mirrors come from polished tiles.
And this is wonderful and not wonderful at all, nothing special.
Nothing special is not wonderful, it's just nothing special.
Suzuki Roshi has a great way of talking about the specialness and the non-specialness of Buddhahood.
He says it's like a mother with children.
For the mother, having children is an ordinary, everyday thing, with all the ups and downs and richness of that, wonderful, annoying, challenging, but ordinary.
The kids are just the kids.
But we just have to take a little teeny step back, the backward step, to remember and just be blown away that that's even possible.
That people could bring new people into the world, babies, children, new lives, manifesting the energy of life, taking a new form.
How is that even possible?
It's shockingly amazing.
And really, mothers and fathers and all of us should just be blinded by the brilliance of that all the time.
Which we are, and we're not.
Ordinary and a miracle.
A miracle and ordinary.
I don't know if this kind of talk is all that useful.
I don't think I'm giving us anything very concrete to work with or apply to life or practice.
And problems, I have plenty of problems, we all have problems.
But maybe such talk isn't about being useful.

Maybe such talk and teachings, as imperfect as they are because of the delivery system of words, are actually kind of like a sort of counterweight to that powerful desire for everything to be useful, everything to make sense, everything to be sensible, understandable, applicable.
I hang around the periphery of the sciences a little bit and of business and organizations.
These wonderful, horrible phrases, like "outcome-oriented" and "evidence-based."
Which is true enough in the hamster wheel of samsara.
But ultimately, so damaging, right?
If life is only that, we lose our humanity.
And the wonder of the children will never be seen.
So it's good to have useful talk about practice.
But it's also a kind of feeding of thinking-thinking.
And there's some useful stuff, like in Fukan Zazengi, it tells you how to arrange your robes and cross your legs.
He's not that far.

But really, it seems like Dogen's teachings and the teachings of his descendants, down to Suzuki Roshi, Norman, me, you, are calling on us to think not thinking, with these teachings that can't be held in think-thinking.
Later in his career, Dogen wrote the essays in Shobogenzo that we study the most often, mostly pretty early in his career.
And he had this huge spurt, right, as he was shifting from the outskirts of Kyoto to the mountains of Echizen, where they made Eiheiji.
And actually, that's a wild part of his life story, just a sidebar there.
There's some, I forget how many months, six months, nine months, where they were camping out.

We don't know any of the details, really, but maybe they were being put up in people's village homes or built rough shelters or something, while Eiheiji was being built, because they were homeless monks.
And in that period, Dogen wrote like a third of Shobogenzo, just cranked it out.
It's unbelievable.
My tendency, maybe yours too, is, "Oh, things are kind of disrupted right now, I really can't focus that much, I'll get to that later," right?
No, he's like...
But anyway.
Later, after Eiheiji was established, he didn't do such long talks anymore or write such long essays on the main.
He wrote a lot about the temple procedures.
But his teachings actually shifted to very short dharma talks called Jodo, which roughly means dharma hall discourse, dharma hall talk.
And the emphasis in these little Jodo talks is nothing but examples of non-thinking.
It doesn't explain much in those.
Here's one that [unclear: "Teigen"] quotes in the great Zazen as an enactment ritual essay, so it came to my attention.
There are hundreds of them.
I have the big fat book, but I haven't really done much with it.
Anyway, here's one of the dharma talks, short dharma talks called Jodo.
The teacher, Dogen, would sit on a high platform, pretty high up, like six feet in the air or something, and the monks would actually stand, didn't sit, to receive the talk in the dharma hall.
That's where they also do service, so there are usually no cushions there.
We're lucky we have cushions.
Anyway, here's the entire talk.
*As this mountain monk, meaning him, today gives a dharma hall discourse, all Buddhas in the three times also today give a dharma discourse.
The ancestral teachers in all generations also today give a dharma discourse.
Already together, having given a dharma hall discourse, what dharma has been expounded?
No other dharma is expressed, but this very dharma is expressed.
What is this dharma?
It is upheld within the monk's hall, it is upheld within the Buddha hall.*
That's the whole talk.
As I give this talk, Buddhas in all directions give talks, the ancestral teachers give talks, and now we have given the talk.
What talk was given?
The dharma was expounded.
This very dharma, what is it?
It is upheld.
Here and there, everywhere.
The dharma is already upheld, already clear, already expounded.
Why would we need to try to explain what it is?
So it's a talk without content.
It's a talk about a talk.
Suzuki Roshi gets at it this way.
*In the Parinirvana Sutra, Buddha says everything has Buddha nature, but Dogen reads it another way.
Everything is Buddha nature.
There is a difference.
If you say everything has Buddha nature, it means Buddha nature is in each existence, so Buddha nature and existence are different.
But when you say everything is Buddha nature, it means everything.
Everything is Buddha nature itself.
To be a human being is to be a Buddha, even though you do not do anything, you are not actually doing something, you are expressing your true nature.
The most important thing is to express your true nature.
With your eyes, your voice, your demeanor, express your Buddha nature in the simplest, most adequate way, and appreciate it in the smallest existence.*
That's nice advice, huh?
Express your Buddha nature because you are Buddha in the simplest, most adequate way, and appreciate it in the smallest existence.
*While you are continuing this practice week after week, year after year, your experience will become deeper and deeper.
Your experience will cover everything you do in everyday life.
The most important thing is to forget all gaining ideas, all dualistic views.
Just practice Zazen in a certain posture.
Remain on your cushions without expecting anything, and you will resume your true nature.
That is to say, your true nature resumes itself.*
Beautiful, huh?
So maybe that's the point of all this.

Making space for your true nature to resume itself, to express itself, so we show up, we think not thinking with strong effort and no expectations, we engage with each other and the world, we see everything and everything as Buddha nature, not having Buddha nature, but as Buddha nature, as Buddha, including things that are hard, things that we detest, things that we love, and things so small we might not notice them.
Do you notice that little bit in there?
Appreciate even the smallest existence.
And just to wrap this up, going back to the end of the Matsu-Nanyue story.
The teacher, Nanyue, after Matsu is confounded and silent, not sure what to do or say, asks the student about cause and effect, about his assumptions about cause and effect.
That's what this question seems to be.
When driving a cart, if it stops moving, you whip the cart or the ox.
How do you understand cause and effect?
And Matsu for sure realized the obvious cause and effect: hit the ox.
How could hitting the cart make any sense?
But he could feel, I think we can feel, that's not the whole story, that a life of only hitting the ox is an incomplete life.
It's a shallow life of suffering, really.
So he was silent.
And so Nanyue closed the encounter, as we have it here anyway, by saying, if you practice Zen, you practice, sorry, if you practice sitting Zen, you practice sitting Buddha.
So this is important, I think.
When we honor this tradition, we practice it by sitting Zazen, sitting Zen, which is literally what that means.
Zah just means to sit, an everyday word for sit.
Sitting Zen, sitting Buddha.
And Dogen reminds us in several of these, and [unclear: "the teacher sees quoting from before or two"], that sitting does not just mean this particular way of arranging the body.
That's just a convention.
We practice not thinking in any posture, all the postures.
So that could be another misconception, that if we have some trouble, back trouble, it's inevitable, right?
Many of our Sangha members have problems with the body.
So not to think that we have to take a certain posture to sit Zen.
It's only to engage in this way.

And Dogen closes the Zazenshin essay by quoting a long poem by a master he really admired named Hongzhi, who was just a little bit before him, born 70, 80 years before him in the 12th century in China.
Dogen was pretty grouchy about a lot of teachers, but he really admired Hongzhi.
And I think Hongzhi actually taught at the same monastery where Dogen went.
I need to double check that.
He actually lived and taught at Tiantang, where Dogen studied with Rujing.
So maybe he felt especially close to him, having been in his same place.
I won't get into it now.
It would require a couple more talks, but Dogen does a long section on Hongzhi's poem about Zazen and does long comments about every line.
But then he offers his own version.
That's the neat thing.
I want to close with that.
It's shorter, which is interesting.
So this is Dogen's version of Hongzhi's poem Zazen Xin, The Point of Zazen.
Interestingly, the point business here is a little hard phrase to translate, because Zazen Xin, the Xin in this case, is not the Xin of heart-mind like in the Heart Sutra.
It's another Xin.
This Xin is the word for a bamboo acupuncture needle.
It's an acupuncture needle.
So literally he's saying Zazen acupuncture needle.
So the point of Zazen.
And I thought that's kind of perfect, actually, for us.
Because acupuncture works within its own understanding, the Chinese medicine understanding of qi, energy, running through the body, running through the meridian pathways in the body.
So clearly there's something to that.
It measurably affects people's health, and health insurance is even starting to pay for acupuncture.
But these meridians and this qi cannot be observed or understood by science at all.
Well, they have various brain studies.
They're into neuroscience, right?
So maybe you can see things that happen in our brains, but you can't see acupuncture working in the brain scanner, or any kind of scanner, I mean.
And yet it does, right?
That's kind of great, huh?
That's kind of like Zazen.
We can't understand it from our scientific, western, rational, useful frame.
And yet, "it works" isn't the right word, but you know what I mean.
Here's Dogen's poem, Zazen Xin, The Point of Zazen.
*The hub of Buddha's activity, the turning of the ancestor's hub, like a hub and a wheel, moves along with beyond thinking, and is completed in the realm of beyond merging.
As it moves along with beyond thinking, its appearing is immediate, its appearance is immediate.
As it is completed in the realm of beyond merging, completeness itself is realization.
When its appearance is immediate, you have no illusion.
When completeness reveals itself, is neither real nor apparent.
When you have immediacy without illusion, immediacy is dropping away, dropping away with no obstacles.
Realization, beyond real, beyond apparent, is effort without expectation.
Clear water all to the bottom, a fish swims like a fish, vast sky transparent throughout, a bird flies like a bird.*
So we have to spend a lot of time on those first lines, but the last three are pretty clear, I think.
Let's hear those again, the last three lines of this.
*Realization, beyond real or apparent, is effort without expectation.
Clear water all the way to the bottom, a fish swims like a fish, vast sky transparent throughout, a bird flies like a bird.*
Stop the recording there.
